description:
Serpstat Group Buy is an option to compare if you want to see which search topics competing websites cover and decide where your own pages could improve. Start with one market, one product or service, and a few domains that appear for searches you actually want to target. Use the results to build a shortlist you can verify.

Serpstat offers its own service. This SEOGBTools listing is a separate third-party offer. Confirm the features, usage limits, and access instructions for the work you need to do.

Choose search competitors for one topic

Start with a product or service you sell and write down several ways a customer might search for it. Open those results in the intended market. A search competitor is a site that shows up for the same topics, even if you do not compete directly for customers in other channels. A marketplace, comparison site, and specialist blog can each compete with a different type of page.

Choose a few domains or URLs that match the type of work you want to do. If your project is a local service page, focus on relevant results that serve the same area. If you are planning a guide, include strong guides. A domain may show up for many topics outside your business. Keep comparisons tied to the topic and market you can actually serve.

Write down why each competitor belongs in the comparison. You may pick one because its categories answer specific shopping needs, another because its guides explain common questions, and a third because it serves your local market. Those notes make the keyword list easier to interpret later.

Find gaps and group them by purpose

Serpstat's keyword gap report uses its regional keyword database to compare the searches for which different domains appear. Treat a missing term as a lead to investigate. Your site might cover the same idea with a different phrase, appear outside the report's range, or have an appropriate page that needs clearer coverage. Open your own page list before deciding to build anything new.

Group phrases according to the task the searcher wants to complete. For a furniture shop, small desks for home offices could belong on a collection page. How to measure a desk for a small room could belong in a guide. Questions about delivery may fit a shipping page or a short answer near the buying controls. When several phrases need the same answer, group them together.

Watch for gaps that do not fit your offer. A competitor might rank for second-hand furniture while you sell new furniture only. A directory might have pages for areas you do not serve. Filtering out terms that are outside your reach can save more writing time than finding hundreds of extra ideas.

Check the live results before writing

Open the strongest candidate searches and note which page types appear. If results mostly show product collections, shoppers may want to compare available items. A long article can be useful as supporting content, but the category should help someone browse and decide. If results mostly show tutorials, the reader may need instructions they can follow before they are ready to buy.

Look for useful details that the existing results leave unclear. A guide to choosing a small desk might include standard measurements but skip where to allow room for a chair. If you can demonstrate that with measurements from products you sell, your page can add something practical. Record the evidence you can contribute before deciding what the article should say.

Check more than the first result when the page type is unclear. A mixed result can mean that searchers have several goals. Choose the part of the task your page can serve well and give readers an obvious link to the next step. Keep the language of the page natural and avoid repeating minor variants that all mean the same thing.

Update an existing page or create a new one?

Check whether you already have a page that should answer the question. If the page gets impressions but misses a useful section, improve it first. A chart, comparison, clearer heading, or internal link may help. A new page makes sense when the search needs a different answer or a separate action, such as browsing a different range of products.

For an existing page, use Search Console to see which searches bring impressions and clicks. Compare that with the competitor ideas. If two pages from your own site serve the same query, read them side by side and decide whether each has a distinct purpose. Check their internal links and where a reader should go after opening each page.

Build a brief with the proposed URL, intended reader, key question, examples to include, and related pages to link. Give the writer the reason a term matters. A brief that only lists keywords may produce content with no clear job. A brief with a real buyer question and a useful example can guide the writer through the entire article.

Use metrics to narrow the list

Estimated volume, difficulty, and position can help you decide what to review first. Keep the market and date with the report. Different keyword databases may show different totals and cover different searches. For a page you already own, use actual Search Console data alongside estimates before deciding where to spend time.

A high-volume phrase can be a poor choice if your site cannot help the person who searches it. A specific phrase may be valuable if it leads to a product category you can support. Look for fit, evidence, and a clear next action. Prioritize topics where your team can add details you can verify, such as prices, measurements, service areas, or examples from a real process.

Keep a small list of rejected ideas with reasons. If a future export surfaces the same terms, you can avoid repeating the same review. Revisit the list when your product range, audience, or service area changes. This is more useful than collecting another spreadsheet with no connection to the site plan.

Compare access and track the next result

Check whether this offer includes the markets, gap reports, usage limits, and exports your project needs. Serpstat's official plans are separate from this SEOGBTools listing. If you need reports for several countries or projects, test a typical job and confirm the export format before relying on it for a deadline.

After publishing a page update, record the date and compare search visibility over a sensible period. Track which URL appears for the topic, whether relevant queries gain impressions, and whether people reach the page you intended. Note site changes and seasonal demand when interpreting movement.

Start with a page sample before comparing entire domains

If you need to improve a category, choose comparable pages and inspect what they cover. Compare product range, pricing presentation, navigation, and the information visitors can use to make a choice. A large competitor may rank for broad searches because it has many categories. A smaller specialist can still compete for a well-defined group of searches when its page offers a more useful selection or clearer details.

Use domain-level research to discover patterns, then narrow the review to relevant URLs. Write down where a competitor uses a guide, category, or product page. If several sites use a similar page type, check whether it fits your own offer. If they differ, look at the details of the search and the market before deciding what to build.

Bring your existing site structure into the review. A site with a useful product category may need better supporting pages and links. A site with a guide that attracts shoppers may need a stronger path from the guide to the products. The right response depends on what visitors need after opening the page.

Example keyword gap review for a service business

Imagine a local painting business wants more exterior enquiries. A competitor comparison surfaces searches about painting brick, preparing wooden surfaces, and the best time of year to paint outside. Open the results and note which terms show service pages and which show advice articles. Then compare those results with the business's existing pages.

A search about whether brick can be painted may belong in a guide if readers want to understand materials and preparation. A search for exterior painters in a city may belong on a service page with the service area, examples, and a quote path. If the business does not offer a particular coating or surface treatment, leave that term out of the commercial page and avoid implying that the service is available.

Use the findings to build a small plan. Update the exterior page with confirmed service details. Add an advice section or article if the team can answer common preparation questions. Link the advice to the service page where a reader would reasonably want a quote. Measure each page against the job it serves.

Make the brief useful to the people doing the work

Send the writer a specific question, the intended visitor, and the page where the answer should appear. Include a few competitor URLs as examples, but explain what your own page can contribute. If the page needs product measurements, verified pricing, or a client example, identify who can supply those details before drafting begins.

List internal links with their purpose. For example, a measuring guide can link to a product category once the reader knows which size they need. A buying guide can link to a delivery policy when shipping limits matter. A link should help the visitor complete the next step rather than interrupt the explanation.

Give the reviewer a clear way to check the draft. Confirm that it answers the main question, the examples are supported, and the intended link opens the right page. Review the headings and first paragraphs as a visitor would. A page that answers the main question early can still offer detail further down for readers who need it.

Return to the gap report after you have evidence

After the update, compare the intended page with the queries that bring impressions. Check whether the page appearing in search matches your plan. If a different page appears, compare both pages and the current results before editing either. You may find the query belongs to a different type of page or that the site gives stronger signals for the other URL.

Review the gap report again when your site adds products or enters a market. A previously rejected term may now fit the offer. Keep records of which country, date, and competitors were used so you can compare similar reports. Changing all three at once can make the new export look more different than it really is.

Treat competitor research as one source alongside customer questions, internal search, and first-party search data. If the same problem appears in several sources, it can be worth addressing even if the estimated search volume is small. If only the export suggests a topic and your site has nothing useful to add, leave it for later.

Run a small access test before committing

Choose a keyword gap comparison in your target market and complete it from start to finish with information you are allowed to use. Compare your site with two sites that appear for a relevant search. Check whether you can filter the results to terms your business can serve. Save the region and the compared domains with your shortlist. Reopen the live results for a few terms before deciding whether to update a page or create one.

Before you order, ask which part of that test the current offer supports and what happens if access is interrupted. Keep your notes and any permitted exports in your own project records so you can continue the work later. Record the planned next step separately from the tool report, especially if another person will make the change.

Related SEO tools

Compare Keywords Everywhere Group Buy and Seobility Group Buy if your workflow includes a follow-up audit or additional keyword research.

Frequently asked questions

What is a keyword gap? It is a difference between the searches covered by compared sites in a particular report. Check the results and your own pages before treating a gap as a new page requirement.

Can I compare competitors from different countries? Use the region that matches your audience and keep separate notes for each market. The same domain can appear for different searches in different regions.

Should I copy every term from the report? Keep terms that fit an offer and a page you can support. Group queries that call for the same answer and discard the ones outside your scope.

What should I verify before ordering? Check the available databases, reports, export options, and usage limits for the type of comparison you run most often.
